Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant/applicant submits that the captioned appeal, filed under Section 415(2) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (hereinafter "BNSS") impugns judgment on conviction dated 06.06.2025 and the order on sentence dated 08.07.2025, passed by the Court of learned Special Judge (PC Act), Coal Block Cases-02, CBI, Rouse Manoj Kumar Jayaswal vs Central Bureau Of Investigation on 4 September, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/161547659/

sentences.text: Vide the order on sentence, the appellant/applicant has been sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years and to pay a fine of 5,00,000/- for the offence punishable under Section 120-B/420 of the IPC and further sentenced rigorous imprisonment for three years and to pay fine of 5,00,000/- for the substantive offence punishable under Section 420 of the IPC in CC No. CBI/297/2019 arising out of RC No. 219 2012 E 0008 CBI/EOU-IV dated 03.09.2012 registered by EOU-IV, CBI, New Delhi.
All sentences would run concurrently.

9. It is submitted that the present application has been filed under Section 430(2) of the BNSS seeking suspension of sentence awarded vide order dated 08.07.2025, passed by the learned Special Judge.
10. The applicant is aged about 70 years, has deep roots in society, and suffers from serious spinal ailments requiring regular medical care.

He has been permitted to travel abroad even during trial,
and has never misused the liberty granted to him.
He remained on bail throughout investigation and trial, and was never arrested at any stage.
This itself shows that he is not a flight risk.

The applicant has cooperated fully with investigation and trial, never violated bail conditions,
and was granted bail on the very first date of appearance.
The alleged acts relate back to the year 2004, i.e., more than twenty years ago.

The applicant has already undergone immense hardship of prolonged litigation for over a decade, and there is no apprehension of tampering with evidence or repeating the alleged offence, since the coal block allocation policy has been completely revised by the Government of India.
12. It is submitted that the applicant has already deposited the fine amount as imposed by the learned trial court.
This shows bona fide conduct and compliance with judicial directions.
Once the fine is paid and the appeal is admitted, there is no justification in insisting on incarceration pending appeal.

During the course of arguments, the applicant has handed over a receipt dated 02.09.2025,
indicating deposit of the fine amount to the tune of Rs.10,00,000/-.
The same is taken on record.
13. It is further submitted that the applicant has strong family ties and social roots.
His wife is dependent on him, and his children and grandchildren live in India.
He has a fixed place of residence at Nagpur, and there is no possibility of his absconding or evading the process of law.
Courts have consistently considered such strong community ties as important factors favouring suspension of sentence.

16. Learned counsel appearing for Central Bureau of Investigation, on advance notice, accepts notice and vehemently opposed the present application for suspension of sentence submitting to the effect that the impugned judgment and order on sentence has been passed in accordance with the law and there is no illegality of any kind thereto.

17. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the material on record.
18.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sudhir Kumar Jain v. State of Delhi (MANU/SC/8988/2007),
observed that Section 389 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (now Section 430 of the BNSS)
empowers the Appellate Courts to suspend sentences till the pendency of appeal where period of sentence does not exceed 3 years.

entities.text: Sudhir Kumar Jain v. State of Delhi (MANU/SC/8988/2007)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
For ease of reference, the relevant observations are reproduced as under:
a. "6.

Keeping in view the fact that the appeals are not being disposed of expeditiously by Appellate Courts, Legislature, in its wisdom, has enacted Section 389, Code of Criminal Procedure Sub-section (3) of which empowers the Trial Court to suspend the sentence of such convicts, who have been convicted for a period not exceeding three years, for such period as will afford them sufficient time to present an appeal.

Section 389 also empowers the Appellate Court including the High Court to suspend the sentence and release the convict on bail during the pendency of the appeal in case the period of sentence does not exceed three years."
19.
The controlling principles regarding suspension of sentence are settled by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.

For suspension of sentences, the Court has long held that suspension should ordinarily be considered liberally so that the statutory right of appeal is meaningful and not rendered illusory by efflux of time.

Most recently, the Supreme Court has reiterated and applied this very approach in Aasif @
Pasha v. State of U.P., 2025 INSC 944.

entities.text:
Aasif @
Pasha v. State of U.P., 2025 INSC 944
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Dealing with a four-year fixed-term sentence, the Hon'ble Court corrected the High Court for refusing suspension, emphasized that appeals are unlikely to be heard promptly, and directed that fixed-term sentences be suspended "liberally unless there are exceptional circumstances".
The Court also reminded that reasons must be recorded, and that the inquiry at this stage is limited.

21. At the same time, it is to be kept in mind that post-conviction suspension stands on a different footing from pre-trial bail, and that appellate courts must not re-appreciate the entire evidence when considering suspension of sentence.
22. In the present case, the applicant has been convicted effectively for a fixed term of three years.

Further, he remained on bail throughout investigation and trial, was never arrested, and has not misused liberty; he is a senior citizen with documented spinal ailments; he has deep social roots and a fixed residence; and he has already deposited the entire fine imposed by the trial court.
These facts are borne out from the record placed with the instant application and diminish any risk of absconding or non-attendance, when the appeal is finally heard.

23. Considering that the effective sentence awarded to the applicant is imprisonment for a period of three years, this Court deems it appropriate to suspend the sentence of the applicant during the pendency of the appeal.

24. Accordingly, sentence awarded to the applicant, i.e., imprisonment of three years is suspended and the applicant is released on bail, subject to his furnishing a bail bond in the sum of Rs.
1,00,000/- with one surety of the like amount, subject to the satisfaction of the Registrar General of this Court This is a digitally signed order.

The application is allowed and disposed of in the afore-mentioned terms.
